study_identification.author_journal_year: Pinaya et al., Human Brain Mapping, 2019
study_identification.title: Using deep autoencoders to identify abnormal brain structural patterns in neuropsychiatric disorders: A large-scale multi-sample study

study_characteristics.study_objective: To use a deep autoencoder trained on healthy controls from the Human Connectome Project to detect and elucidate neuroanatomical deviations in individual patients with schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorder, and to assess whether the model could generate different patterns of neuroanatomical deviations for different diseases.

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: FreeSurfer v5.3.0; Desikan-Killiany atlas for cortical parcellation (68 cortical subregions); whole brain segmentation for subcortical volumes (36 structures)

response_variable.answer: Cortical thickness (68 Desikan-Killiany regions); Subcortical volumes (36 structures); Total 104 brain regions

predictor_effects.answer: Age and sex are incorporated as semi-supervised learning targets. Age modeled as classification (16 classes for ages 22-37). Sex modeled as binary classification. Both variables are part of the latent representation with cross-covariance cost to disentangle from other latent features.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study incorporates age and sex as confounding variables within the semi-supervised learning framework and applies L2 regularization and denoising with additive Gaussian noise. However, site effects are not explicitly modeled despite using data from different scanners (HCP data collected on Siemens Skyra 3T, NUSDAST on Siemens MAGNETOM VISION, ABIDE from 20 different sites). The authors acknowledge this limitation and restrict statistical comparisons to patient and control groups from the same dataset to avoid site/scanner/population effects. The model uses zero mean unit variance normalization, which helps with heteroscedasticity but doesn't fully address all nuisance structures.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: Similar to Cheung, Livezey, Bansal, and Olshausen (2014), we added information about our samples (in our case, age and sex values) in the structure of the model... The final loss function to train the deep autoencoder is defined as the sum of four separate cost terms... The fourth term XCov is the unsupervised cross-covariance cost which guides the training to select solutions that disentangle the confounding variables (i.e., age and sex) from the other latent features of the data... To avoid the effects of different sites, scanners, and populations, we restricted statistical comparisons to patient and control groups from the same data set.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.location: Main text page 3-4, lines 91-99; page 5, lines 111-112

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study performed 10-fold cross-validation on the HCP training data to select the optimal number of neurons in each hidden layer. This involved dividing the training set into training and validation folds, testing different configurations (ranging from 10 to 100 neurons per layer), and selecting the configuration with the lowest average reconstruction error. The best configuration (104-100-75-100-104) achieved a mean reconstruction error of 0.40±0.01 during cross-validation.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: In this study, the number of neurons per layer was chosen using the training/validation data from the HCP data set. This involved executing a 10-fold cross-validation process where the training set was divided into two groups: training and validation set. Thus, we adopted a grid search to select the optimal number of neurons (i.e., among 10, 25, 50, 75, and 100) in each hidden layer... We defined the optimum model structure as the one that presented the lowest average reconstruction error at the validation folds during the cross-validation process.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.location: Main text page 7, lines 137-138; Supplementary Table 1

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: The study does not report validation using an independent held-out subset of the HCP training data. After selecting the optimal configuration through cross-validation, the deep autoencoder was trained using the entire HCP dataset (all 1,113 subjects). There is no mention of reserving an independent test set from the HCP data for validation purposes before applying the model to the clinical datasets.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: After determining the optimum values, the deep autoencoder was trained again with the best configuration and using both training and validation set... In this analysis, we used the deep autoencoder structure with three hidden layers and the 104-100-75-100-104 configurations. We performed the training on the whole HCP data set.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.location: Main text page 7, lines 137-138; page 7-8, lines 151-152

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The trained normative model was validated on two independent clinical datasets from different domains: NUSDAST (Northwestern University Schizophrenia Data) with 40 HC and 35 SCZ patients, and ABIDE (Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange) with 105 HC and 83 ASD patients. Both datasets were acquired from different scanners and sites than the HCP training data. The model successfully differentiated patients from healthy controls in both datasets (NUSDAST: p=.001, Cliff's delta=0.4142; ABIDE: p<.001, Cliff's delta=0.2764). The study also compared the normative approach performance against traditional SVM classifiers using bootstrap resampling (1,000 repetitions), obtaining AUC-ROC values and 95% confidence intervals.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: After training using the HCP data set, we defined the average squared reconstruction error along all brain features as a metric of brain deviation of each subject... Then, we used the model to measure the quantity of deviation of the brain data from the NUSDAST and ABIDE data sets based on what was learned from the HCP sample... The deep autoencoder yielded a mean deviation metric of 0.97±0.23 for the HC group and 1.14±0.28 for the SCZ group from the NUSDAST data set (Cliff's delta = 0.4142)... In the NUSDAST data set, the linear SVM obtained a median AUC-ROC = 0.637 (95% CI = [0.486, 0.766]), whereas using the deviation metric of the normative approach, we obtained an AUC-ROC = 0.707 (95% CI = [0.662, 0.751]).
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.location: Main text page 5-6, lines 105-112; page 8, lines 158-161; page 8-9, lines 171-196

clinical_dataset.answer: NUSDAST (Northwestern University Schizophrenia Data and Software Tool); ABIDE (Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange)

clinical_groups_age.answer: SCZ: mean 25.5 sd 3.92 min 22 max 36; ASD: mean 27.3 sd 4.1 min 22 max 36

deviation_metric.answer: Mean squared reconstruction error (average squared difference between original and reconstructed values across all 104 brain regions)

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Mann-Whitney U test to compare median deviation metrics between HC and patient groups within each dataset. Cliff's delta absolute value to measure effect size. Regional analysis: Mann-Whitney U test with conservative threshold p<.01 (expected false positive rate 1%), Cliff's delta to quantify regional deviations. Comparison with SVM classifier using bootstrap resampling (1,000 repetitions) to estimate AUC-ROC and 95% confidence intervals.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: The deep autoencoder successfully generated significantly different deviation metrics for SCZ and ASD patients compared to their respective healthy control groups, revealing distinct neuroanatomical patterns consistent with existing literature, though with modest discriminative performance (AUC-ROC 0.64-0.71).
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: The deep autoencoder yielded significantly higher mean deviation metrics in both patient groups compared to their respective controls: SCZ showed 1.14±0.28 vs HC 0.97±0.23 (p=.001, Cliff's delta=0.4142), and ASD showed 1.27±0.40 vs HC 1.09±0.30 (p<.001, Cliff's delta=0.2764). Regional analysis revealed disease-specific patterns: in SCZ, the most altered regions included left lateral ventricle (effect size=0.410), left ventral diencephalon (0.417), right superior temporal cortex (0.387), and left precentral cortex (0.319), consistent with known schizophrenia findings. In ASD, significant alterations were found in left choroid plexus (0.250), right cuneus (0.245), left putamen (0.228), and left cerebellum cortex (0.222). The normative approach achieved AUC-ROC of 0.707 (95% CI [0.662, 0.751]) for SCZ and 0.639 (95% CI [0.611, 0.666]) for ASD, comparable to or slightly better than traditional SVM classifiers (0.637 and 0.569, respectively). Age prediction had MAE of 3.40 years (HC) and 3.57 years (SCZ) for NUSDAST, and 4.02 years (HC) and 3.83 years (ASD) for ABIDE. Sex prediction accuracies ranged from 62-79% across groups.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: The model showed modest discriminative performance, with high within-group variability in deviation metrics, likely reflecting clinical and neuroanatomical heterogeneity. The use of regional features (rather than voxel-based) may limit sensitivity due to dimensionality reduction during preprocessing. The nonlinear nature of the model prevents establishing direction of alterations (increase vs decrease). Potential confounds from head motion differences between patients and controls were not explicitly addressed. Automatic preprocessing without manual quality control may introduce artifacts, particularly in samples with ventricular enlargement. Different acquisition protocols and scanners across datasets were not modeled, restricting direct cross-dataset comparisons. The semi-supervised approach for handling age/sex as confounds differs from standard neuroimaging practices and requires further investigation.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The deep autoencoder framework demonstrates flexibility for different neuroimaging modalities and preprocessing approaches. Unlike traditional normative approaches, it generates individualized brain maps showing each region's contribution to the deviation metric, providing mechanistic insights while maintaining some interpretability challenges inherent to deep neural networks. Guided backpropagation with SmoothGrad technique was used to assess feature importance, revealing that the model learned non-trivial representations (not simply copying inputs). The model showed sex influences volumetric measures (structures not normalized by intracranial volume). Comparison with PCA showed that while PCA achieved lower reconstruction error in healthy subjects (0.0355 vs 0.32), the deep autoencoder achieved larger effect sizes in differentiating patients from controls.

general_notes.general_notes: This is one of the early applications of deep autoencoders for normative modeling in neuroimaging. The study uses a denoising autoencoder approach with additive Gaussian noise (mean=0, SD=0.1) during training to improve robustness. The architecture includes three hidden layers (h1: 100 neurons, z: 75 neurons, h2: 100 neurons) with SELU activation functions for faster convergence and regularization. Training used Adam optimizer with learning rate decay (0.05 to 0.0005), L2 regularization (1×10^-3), mini-batch size of 64, and 2,000 epochs. The semi-supervised framework incorporates age and sex predictions as auxiliary tasks with cross-entropy loss and cross-covariance cost for disentanglement. All data were normalized using zero mean unit variance from HCP statistics. For ABIDE, subjects were selected from 20 different sites within the age range 22-37 to match HCP. NUSDAST data were acquired on a Siemens MAGNETOM VISION with different parameters than HCP (Siemens Skyra 3T). The study acknowledges that multivariate methods can detect effects based on either mean differences or changes in inter-regional correlations, explaining why some regions showed significant deviations but not in univariate analysis. Bootstrap resampling used 70% training set split with 1,000 repetitions for classifier evaluation. Saliency maps (Supplementary Figure 2-3) revealed that age-informative regions included pallidum, brain stem, corpus callosum, hippocampus, while sex-informative regions included optic chiasm, amygdala, cerebellum cortex, temporal pole, caudate, ventricles.
